div.p: Compositional real-time scheduling frameworks provide ways for building large and complex real-time embedded systems from independent sub-systems. This paper introduces a novel scheme for scheduling a component of Mixed-Criticality (MC) sporadic tasks on uniprocessor system. It characterizes the mixed criticality resource allocations, and the interface model for abstracting the real-time requirements of such a component. The demand bound function and supply bound function for the low and high criticality modes are derived to determine the schedulability of a component in both modes. The execution times of jobs are monitored in this approach. If it is detected that the behavior of system is inconsistent with low criticality level, then tasks of low criticalities are discarded and the priorities of high criticality tasks are re-ordered in high criticality mode to guarantee the schedulabilty of high criticality tasks. We propose a new algorithm, which schedules a component of mixed criticality jobs in low mode through MC Rate Monotonic (MC-RM) algorithm by applying period transformation, and guarantees the schedulabilty by using MC Earliest Deadline First (MC-EDF) algorithm in high mode.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Mixed-criticality systems integrate tasks with different safety requirements or functionalities on the same platform, to meet rapidly increasing cost, weight, power and thermal constraints. Such different functionalities are not equally critical or important to the overall performance of the system. For example, it is more important that the control system of an unmanned aerial vehicle guarantees the correctness for the flight critical functionalities such as vehicle safety than the mission critical functionalities like images capturing during the execution of surveillance missions. Therefore, there is a need to guarantee the simultaneous temporal correctness of all the different criticalities at the respective criticality levels. For the most critical functionalities, it is required to guarantee temporal correctness under exceedingly pessimistic assumptions which may be very unlikely to occur in reality (e.g. worst case execution times calculated from static analysis). It is also needed to guarantee the correctness of all the different functionalities under less pessimistic assumptions (e.g. worst case execution times from measurements).

Component-based design is a widely accepted methodology for building a large real-time system through systematic abstraction and composition by using component interfaces. In such a system, the real-time requirements (i.e. the total resource demand and workload deadlines) of each component must be guaranteed. This approach has the added advantages of reusability. The components are organized in a tree like structure known as hierarchical scheduling framework and these real-time components share system resources under different scheduling policies. Many such frameworks [1,2,3,4,5] have been proposed for various real-time models. In [1], a hierarchical real-time virtual resource model is introduced that has extended resource partitions to multiple levels. A periodic resource model [2,3,5] for the compositional hierarchical framework is proposed to handle the periodic task model in [6]. These resource models explore the behavior of periodic resource and compute its minimum resource allocations. However, a specific attention is not given to port the mixedcriticality task model in compositional framework. Therefore, it is legitimate to provide solutions for composing and handling the growing complexity of large real-time systems based on mixed criticalities. Thus, the basic goal of this research is to develop and analyze compositional scheduling framework to support the mixed criticality task model.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Vestal [7] introduced mixed-criticality scheduling and extended fixed-priority response-time analysis of sporadic tasks to schedule such systems [7]. Later on, Dorin, et al. [8] proved that the Vestal algorithm is optimal in the domain of fixed-task-priority preemptive algorithms. But according to Baruah and Vestal [9], if one is not restricted to fixed-task priority preemptive algorithms, then the algorithm in [7] is not optimal and is also incomparable with the EDF algorithm. Then, Baruah, et al. [10] improved Vestal scheduling. Baruah, et al. showed that even if the mixed-criticality jobs are released at the same time, the optimal schedulability of such task set is strongly NP-hard [11]. Later on, [12] they proposed a heuristic algorithm OCBP, in which jobs are assigned priorities using a variant of the Audsley approach [13]. OCBP is very effective for scheduling the task sets on 1.618 speed processor. One can also derive a load bound for OCBP from it [12]. Baruah, et al. also refined the bound for OCBP [14]. They also extended the results in [12] to an arbitrary number of criticality levels [15]. Li and Baruah (LB) [16] extended this heuristic scheduling strategy to mixed criticality sporadic task systems. LB computes and assigns priorities to jobs in a busy period. But the major problem with this strategy is that it requires a lot of computation for runtime decisions by the scheduler. Guan, et al. improved it to some extent and presented an OCBP-based scheduler having polynomial complexity [17] for runtime decisions by the scheduler.

An implicit-deadline scheduling algorithm called EDF-VD [18] is proposed by Baruah, et al. for mixed criticality sporadic task sets. In this algorithm the period of each highcriticality task is splitted into two parts for each of the two virtual deadlines. In the schedulability analysis, these different periods are used in different criticality modes. If the utilization of the mixed-criticality task set is sufficiently low, then task set is considered schedulable. Ekberg and Yi [19,20] have used an EDF like approach for scheduling mixed criticality sporadic task sets. They have used EDF to derive demand bound functions for the schedulability of the task set. Tasks have different demand bound functions for each criticality mode, due to different deadlines. An efficient Greedy scheduling algorithm is used to shape the demand of task set to the available resource supply by tuning relative deadlines. In this paper, we have also derived demand bound functions and supply bound functions for scheduling mixed criticality sporadic task sets. This new approach has benefits and features of the compositional hierarchical real-time scheduling.

div.head: III. COMPOSITIONAL REAL-TIME SCHEDULING FRAMEWORK FOR MIXED-CRITICALITY SYSTEMS
div.p: The research in this paper is focus on the scheduling of MC sporadic tasks on a preemptive uniprocessor system in a compositional framework. A MC sporadic task potentially releases an infinite sequence of MC jobs like a traditional non MC real-time systems.

div.head: A. MC Jobs
div.p: The job in an MC system is defined by the following 5tuple of parameters: J i = (a i , d i , c i (Lo), c i (Hi), cl i ), where
• a i ∈ R+ denotes the release time.
• d i ∈ R+ is the absolute deadline.
• c i (Lo) ∈ R+ specifies the worst case execution time (WCET) estimate of job J i in Low Criticality mode.
• c i (Hi) ∈ R+ specifies the WCET estimate of job J i in High Criticality mode.
• cl i ∈ {Lo, Hi} is the criticality of the job, where Lo and Hi denote the Low and High criticalities, respectively.

div.head: B. MC Tasks
div.p: Each task τ i in a MC sporadic task set is characterized by the following 5-tuple of parameters: τ i = (P i , D i , C i (Lo), C i (Hi), CL i ), where • P i ∈ R+ is the period of the task, which is the minimum inter release separation time between successive jobs of the task.
• D i ∈ R+ is the relative deadline.
• C i (Lo) ∈ R+ is the WCET estimate in Lo criticality mode.
• C i (Hi) ∈ R+ is the WCET estimate in Hi criticality mode.
• CL i ∈ {Lo, Hi} denotes the criticality level of the task, where Lo specifies the Lo criticality and Hi specify the Hi criticality for the task.

In this research, the schedulability of scheduling component is defined with the notion that resource model R supplies resource in worst case scenario. The proposed compositional framework overview is demonstrated by the example of Figure 1. Scheduling components are organized in a hierarchical manner, in which resource is supplied from a parent component to the child component. Both components C 1 and C 2 have two mixed criticality tasks each. Interfaces I 1 and I 2 are derived from the characteristics of components C 1 and C 2 , respectively. These interfaces of the lower layer components are considered as corresponding tasks, i.e., τ 5 and τ 6 for the upper layer component C 0 .

Initially, when the system is in low criticality mode then all the low and high criticality tasks are scheduled using MC-RM (MC Rate Monotonic) scheduling algorithm by applying period transformation. The advantage of using this algorithm in the low criticality mode is that high criticality tasks have higher execution priorities than low criticality tasks after period transformation. When the system is switched into the high criticality mode then the low criticality tasks are discarded and only high criticality tasks are scheduled using MC-EDF (MC-Earliest Deadline First) scheduling algorithm. The advantage of using this algorithm in the high criticality mode is that high criticality tasks have low execution demand as compare to MC-RM algorithm. Now, upper layer component C 0 schedules these two tasks without considering the scheduling information of its child components. As a result, the component C 0 allocates resource supply R 1 and R 2 to the two lower layer components C 1 and C 2 , respectively. • Θ(Hi) is the resource allocation time per period in high criticality mode (0 < Θ(Hi) ≤ Π).

In compositional real-time scheduling framework, it is necessary to calculate accurately the resource supply of a resource model [3]. A mixed-criticality resource model Γ guarantees minimum resource supply of Θ(Lo) in low criticality mode for every Π time units. The supply bound function sbf Γ(Lo) (t) defines the minimum resource supply for a mixed-criticality resource model Γ(Π, Θ(Lo), Θ(Hi)) in low criticality mode. It is defined by the following Equation as in [5].
div.formula: sbf Γ(Lo) (t) = ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ t -(k + 1)(Π -Θ(Lo)) if t ∈ [(k + 1)Π -2Θ(Lo), (k + 1)Π -Θ(Lo)], (k -1)Θ(Lo) otherwise,(1)
where k = max( (t -(Π -Θ(Lo)))/Π , 1), 0 < t ≤ St + RHi Π.
div.p: St is the switch time form low to high criticality mode, and RHi is the ratio between C i (Lo) and C i (Hi).

Similarly, the supply bound function sbf ΓHi (t) defines the minimum resource supply for a mixed-criticality resource model Γ(Π, Θ(Lo), Θ(Hi)) in high criticality mode for the time interval t, as given in Equation (2).
div.formula: sbf Γ(Hi) (t) = ⎧ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎩ t -(k + 1)(Π -Θ(Hi)) if t ∈ [(k + 1)Π -2Θ(Hi), (k + 1)Π -Θ(Hi)], (k -1)Θ(Hi) otherwise,(2)
div.p: where k = max( (t -(Π -Θ(Hi)))/Π , 1), St + RHi Π < t ≤ LCM . LCM is the least common multiple of P i for all τ i .

div.head: V. DEMAND BOUND FUNCTIONS FOR MIXED-CRITICALITY TASKS
div.p: A demand bound function is used for the schedulability analysis of a real-time mixed-criticality workload [21]. It specifies the maximum execution demand of a real-time workload in any time interval of length t. A mixed-criticality task τ i behaves like a sporadic task in low criticality mode, and all τ i jobs are guaranteed to be executed for at most C i (Lo) time units. Therefore the demand bound function for a workload W in low criticality mode can be computed by using the standard method in [21]. In high criticality mode, one has to consider all those high criticality jobs that are active when the system is switched to high criticality mode, therefore it is more tricky to accurately calculate demand bound function for high criticality.
Definition 1: Carry-over jobs are those jobs of high criticality tasks which are active (unfinished executions) during the switch to high criticality mode.

div.head: A. Demand of the carry-over jobs
div.p: The remaining execution time of the carry-over jobs should be finished before their respective deadlines in the high critical-ity mode. It is necessary to consider the demand of the carryover jobs in the demand bound function of high criticality tasks workload. Conceptually, a carry-over job is a job that is released at the time of switch in the high criticality mode. But, the scheduling window of the carry-over job may be shorter than other jobs of the same task and can therefore is the remaining interval between switch and deadline. The execution demand of such a job will be also be lower than other jobs, because it may have executed for some time in the low criticality mode before the switch. Now, as the system is in high criticality mode, therefore the job should complete C i (Hi) execution time units in total before its deadline.

div.head: B. Adjustment of the carry-over jobs demand
div.p: The major problem arises from the fact that high criticality jobs may be executed quite late by the MC-RM scheduling algorithm in the low criticality mode due to their higher periods. When a system is switched to high criticality mode, a carry-over job has to complete its remaining high criticality worst case execution demand, for which it may have remain very short scheduling window. To mitigate this problem, period transformation is used in the low criticality mode. It is a scheme which modifies a workload in order to get high scheduling priorities for higher criticality tasks [13]. If the period of a higher criticality task is longer than a lower criticality task, run time quantum (time slice) is used for high criticality task to schedule it with the modified smaller period and execution time. When a transformed task is executed in time slice, it will accumulate a total of C i (Lo) execution time by the end of its actual untransformed period. After period transformation, all the transformed periods of a high criticality task have equal sizes, while the WCET estimate C i (Lo) of high criticality tasks are continuously divided into halves and sub halves such that the number of transformed periods and transformed WCET estimate c i (Lo) becomes equal. Similarly, the respective transformed period and WCET estimate C i (Lo) for the low criticality tasks and untransformed high criticality tasks are p i = P i and c i (Lo) = C i (Lo) in the low criticality mode. After the switch, some portions of high criticality tasks will have already executed in the low criticality mode due to high priority than low criticality tasks. Furthermore, higher scheduling window will be available to these jobs in the high criticality to complete their C i (Hi) execution time units in total before their respective deadlines.

Lemma 1: Assume that the proposed algorithm uses transformed period p i and actual period P i for the high criticality task τ i in the low and high criticality modes respectively, and it is guaranteed that the demand is fulfilled in the low criticality mode using transformed periods. If the system is switched from low into high criticality mode then the following hold for a job of task τ i , 3) p i •CJ i < P i : The carry over job has at most P ip i • CJ i remaining scheduling window (CJ i is a counter for the number of transformed executions of a highcriticality job).

Proof: In the first case, the system is switched from low to high criticality mode after all transformed periods of the job. As it is assumed that the demand is fulfilled in low criticality mode using transformed periods, MC-RM algorithm guarantees to finish the C i (Lo) execution time units of the job before its original period (assume period and deadline are equal) in the low criticality mode. Therefore, the carry over job has already finished its C i (Lo) execution before the switch and it further needs only C i (Hi)-C i (Lo) time units for execution in the high mode before its original deadline.

In the second case, the system is switched from low to high criticality mode when the job has not finished its all transformed c i (Lo) execution time units in all the transformed periods of the job. As it is assumed that the demand is fulfilled in low criticality mode using transformed periods, MC-RM algorithm guarantees to finish the n k=1 c i k (Lo) execution time units of the job before its original period( assume period and deadline are equal) in the low criticality mode. Therefore, the carry over job has not finished its C i (Lo) execution before the switch and it further needs C i (Hi)-n k=1 c i k (Lo) time units for execution in the high mode before its original deadline.

In the third case, if the system is switched to high criticality mode while the carry over job has not been executed in its all transformed periods, then the remaining scheduling window of such a job is at most P ip i • CJ i .

div.head: C. Deriving demand bound functions
div.p: The behavior of a mixed-criticality task τ i is like a normal sporadic task in low criticality mode. After period transformation, the demand bound function for a workload W of such tasks under MC-RM algorithm at time interval t is formulated as follow:
div.formula: dbf WLo (A, t) = c i (Lo) + τ k ∈HPW (i) t/p k • c k (Lo),(3)
div.p: where HP W (i) is the set of higher-priority tasks than τ i in W , and 0 < t ≤ St (St is the switch time from low to high criticality mode).
In high criticality mode, the demand bound function for a workload W of tasks under MC-EDF algorithm at time interval t is formulated as follow:
div.formula: full-dbf WHi (A, t) = τi∈Hi(W ) t/P i • C i (Hi),(4)
div.p: where, St < t ≤ LCM W (LCM W is the least common multiple of P i for all τ i ∈ Hi(W )).

This demand bound function uses C i (Hi) for all the jobs of a task in a workload W . It does not consider that carryover jobs have finished some execution in the low-criticality mode. If there are some carry-over jobs then one must subtract the execution times which these jobs have finished before the switch. The following equation quantifies the amount of work finished by these jobs in low mode.
div.formula: done WLo (A, St) = τi∈W n k=1 c i k (Lo)(5)
div.p: Now, the actual demand bound function in high-criticality mode is formulated as follow:
div.formula: dbf WHi (A, t) = full-dbf W (A, t) -done WLo (A, St),(6)
div.p: where, St < t ≤ LCM W .

div.head: VI. THE PROPOSED ALGORITHM
div.p: The proposed mixed-criticality rate monotonic and earliest deadline first (MCRMEDF) algorithm computes the priority order of jobs according to MC-RM algorithm by using the subroutine JobsOrderedByRM(). First the proposed algorithm transforms the periods of the high criticality tasks which have higher periods than the low criticality tasks by using the subroutine PeriodTransformation(). Thus, high criticality tasks have higher priority than low criticality tasks in the low criticality mode.

The schedulability of the jobs are checked with the help of subroutine LoModeFailure(), by using the new priority order in the low criticality mode. If a job misses a deadline, then the job is not schedulable. If the instance is schedulable in the low mode and the system switches to high criticality mode by checking subroutine HiModeSwitch(), then the proposed algorithm computes the priority order of only high criticality jobs, according to MC-EDF algorithm by using subroutine JobsOrderedByEDF() in the high mode. All the low criticality tasks are discarded in the high mode. It is better to use the EDF priority assignment, because when the system is switched to high criticality mode, then the scheduling becomes a single criticality problem, for which EDF is optimal scheduling algorithm.

div.head: VII. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is evaluated on a component workload of characterized mixed criticality task sets. Particularly, the efficiency of this scheme is studied when period transformation is applied to the high criticality tasks in low criticality mode before scheduling the mixed criticality task sets by the scheduling algorithm. This approach uses demand bound function and supply bound function for the acceptance ratio (schedulability) of the schedulability tests.

div.head: A. Task set generation
div.p: Starting with an empty task set, a random task set is generated for a component workload W , to which random tasks are added successively. Each task generation is controlled by parameters PHi, RHi, CLoMax and TMax. The parameter PHi shows the probability of being a high criticality and RHi indicates the maximum ratio between a low and high worst case execution times. CLoMax and TMax represent the maximum worst case execution time and maximum period respectively. A task τ i is randomly generated as follows:
• CL i =Hi with probability PHi that the generated task is a high criticality task, otherwise CL i =Lo.
• C i (Lo) is generated in the range [0.1, CLoMax], mostly in increasing manner between successive tasks.
• C i (Hi) = C i (Lo)• RHi, where RHi is a fixed multiplier (e.g. RHi=1.5). For low criticality task, C i (Hi) = 0.
• Periods are generated in the range with a factor of at most 100 differences between minimum and maximum periods. Mostly, there is uniform difference between successive periods.
• D i = P i , deadline is equal to period.

A task set is generated with a target utilization U * . As it is difficult to generate an exact target utilization, therefore U * is allowed to fall within the small interval between U * min and U * max . Where U * min = U * -0.005 and U * max = U * + 0.005. If the target utilization U * of the generated task set is not in the given interval, then the whole task set is discarded. Similarly, if either U Lo (T ) or U Hi (T ) is greater than 0.68 then the task set is also discarded, where U Lo (T ) and U Hi (T ) are the utilization of low and high criticality tasks respectively, in the generated workload.

div.head: B. Simulation Results
div.p: Figure 3 shows the percentage of task sets generated that are schedulable for a component workload W , under the target utilization. Almost 50% of these tasks having high criticality, i.e., PHi=0.5, and the high criticality execution time is 1.5 times of its low criticality execution time for each high criticality task , i.e. RHi=1.5.

In Figure 4, the effect on schedulability of task sets is shown by varying parameters PHi, RHi and n (the size of task set). The weighted schedulability measure [22] is plot in terms of the varied parameter. The weighted schedulability measure reduces a 3-dimensional plot to 2-dimensional plot. More importance is given to the schedulability measure for a larger utilization, as one is interested in such cases. Figure 4 varies the parameter PHi, i.e. the percentage of high criticality tasks in the task set. Figure 5 varies RHi, the ratio between low and high criticality execution times, and Figure 6 varies the number of tasks in the task sets.

Figure 4 shows a decline in schedulability with increase in the percentage of high criticality tasks. When the ratio between low and high criticality worst case execution times is increased then schedulability decreases as shown in Figure 5. Similarly, if the number of tasks is increased then schedulability is declined as plotted in Figure 6. For schedulability, the demand bound functions and supply bound functions are derived for both the low and high criticality modes. Instead of a single priority per task, new priorities are assigned to the high criticality tasks when there is a criticality mode change. Evaluation shows that the new algorithm performs better for such a system. The scheduling algorithm in this paper has the features of fixed priority scheduler and dynamic priority scheduler, providing relative ease of practical implementation and theoretical analysis of such schedulers. Experimental evaluations indicate the significance of the novel approach.

The proposed algorithm for scheduling a component of mixed criticality sporadic tasks can be extended to more than two levels of criticalities. As future work, one can also investigates such mixed criticality task model, where the jobs have mutual data dependencies. For such variant of scheduling problem, it is necessary to extend the research to multi-core and virtualization systems.
